issues.subcategory: inconsistent operationalization of moral incongruence
issues.description: The manuscript provides contradictory definitions of the focal construct. In most of the paper, moral incongruence is defined as the interaction between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency. However, in the Present Study section it is redefined as the interaction of moral disapproval with severity of consequences from the action. This is not a trivial wording issue because it changes the predictor specification and construct being tested.
issues.quote: "we seek to establish whether moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)" ... "Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action."

issues.subcategory: contradictory administration of key measures
issues.description: The manuscript first states that only participants endorsing past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use, but later states that key measures of problematic use and moral disapproval will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. These contradictory inclusion rules materially affect sample composition, missingness structure, and analytic comparability across outcomes.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use." ... "For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample."

issues.subcategory: sample size inconsistency
issues.description: The target total sample size is described inconsistently. The manuscript reports an exact planned total of 4,000 in the abstract, but in Methods says the total sample will be "over 4,000" even though 2,500 + 1,500 = 4,000. This inconsistency raises uncertainty about actual planned enrollment and power calculations.
issues.quote: "upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500)." ... "This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults."

issues.subcategory: frequency scale coding inconsistency
issues.description: The pornography frequency scale is described in the main text as 1 to 6, whereas the supplemental instrument shows 0 to 5, aligned with other ASSIST-like items. This discrepancy affects inclusion thresholds, centering, interaction construction, and interpretation.
issues.quote: "participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)." ... Supplemental: "Never (0) ... More than Once Per Day (5)"

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measurement contradiction
issues.description: The methods state gambling frequency will be assessed using a single item, but then say an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental instrument appears to contain only one general gambling-frequency item, so there are no multiple gambling behavior items to average. This undermines clarity about the predictor actually analyzed.
issues.quote: "We will assess gambling frequency using a single item." ... "To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken."

issues.subcategory: nicotine variable structure mismatch
issues.description: The manuscript says tobacco and non-cigarette nicotine products will be subsumed by a single question, yet later lists both "tobacco" and "non-tobacco nicotine" among substance outcomes and Table 1 combines them as "Tobacco/Nicotine products." The planned variables are not consistently defined, which affects the stated number of outcomes and the mapping between measures and analyses.
issues.quote: "we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine." ... "Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis)."

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes/analyses inconsistent
issues.description: The manuscript references eight proposed outcomes and eight moderation analyses, but elsewhere the set of behaviors/outcomes is ambiguously enumerated and duplicates some outcomes with both validated scales and modified ASSIST versions. The actual count of primary analyses is therefore unclear, complicating multiplicity and power evaluation.
issues.quote: "assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes." ... "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses" ... Table 1 lists both "Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items" and "Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items"

issues.subcategory: nonrepresentative oversample compromises claimed representativeness
issues.description: The study repeatedly describes itself as using a representative U.S. sample, but one large portion of the sample is an oversample restricted to recent sports-wagering adults. Unless analyses use appropriate survey weighting or are stratified, pooled estimates will not represent the U.S. population. The manuscript does not clearly state whether primary analyses will be weighted or conducted separately by sample frame.
issues.quote: "representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500) and a sample of sports-wagering individuals in the U.S. (n=1,500)." ... "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms."

issues.subcategory: missing weighting/complex survey details
issues.description: Because the sample combines a matched national sample with a targeted sports-wagering oversample, the analysis requires explicit information on sampling weights, post-stratification, and whether estimates are design-corrected. None of this is specified, preventing evaluation of representativeness, standard errors, or the validity of pooled inferences.
issues.quote: "Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms."

issues.subcategory: overclaim from convenience/panel frame to U.S. population
issues.description: The manuscript calls the sample nationally representative, but YouGov panel recruitment and matching are not equivalent to probability sampling. Without caveats about panel-based inference, noncoverage, and self-selection, the paper overstates external validity.
issues.quote: "target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender."

issues.subcategory: oversample of gamblers biases domain comparisons
issues.description: Including a large sports-wagering oversample may distort comparisons across behavior domains because gambling-related norms, moral attitudes, and comorbid addictions may differ systematically from the general population. Without explicit modeling of sample source or interaction by sample frame, cross-domain comparisons may be confounded by recruitment source.
issues.quote: "we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically."

issues.subcategory: cross-domain measures not parallel
issues.description: The central comparison assumes moral incongruence is comparably assessed across pornography, gambling, and substances. However, outcomes differ substantially: BPS for pornography, PGSI for gambling, and modified ASSIST averages for substances; time windows and item content differ; and some outcomes include guilt-laden content while others do not. This threatens the validity of claims that stronger interactions in one domain imply uniqueness of the construct rather than differences in measurement sensitivity or criterion content.
issues.quote: "with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use (the Brief Pornography Screen and the Problem Gambling Severity Index, respectively)."

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence reduced to a product term
issues.description: The manuscript equates moral incongruence with the interaction term of moral disapproval and frequency. But incongruence conceptually refers to mismatch between values and behavior; a product term does not directly index discrepancy and can be high whenever both disapproval and frequency are high, regardless of whether behavior violates a broader value system or identity. This operationalization risks construct underrepresentation and may not justify claims about moral incongruence per se.
issues.quote: "moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use"

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval for each behavior is assessed with a single item. Single-item measures are vulnerable to unreliability and limited content coverage, especially for a construct as nuanced as moral disapproval. Measurement error in a moderator is especially problematic because it attenuates interactions and can produce misleading null or weak effects.
issues.quote: "For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement 'I believe that using ________ is morally wrong' on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree)."

issues.subcategory: outcome contamination by morality/guilt content
issues.description: The outcome measures are not construct-pure with respect to addiction/problem severity. For example, the BPS includes guilt-related content, and PGSI includes feeling guilty. Because guilt and moral disapproval are closely related, predictor-outcome associations may partly reflect semantic overlap rather than a substantive effect of moral incongruence on dysregulation.
issues.quote: BPS item: "You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it." ... PGSI item: "Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?"

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST applied to behaviors without validation
issues.description: The study extends ASSIST items to pornography and gambling and uses averaged modified items as outcomes, despite acknowledging these adaptations are unvalidated. This creates unknown psychometric properties and undermines cross-domain comparability, especially when those adapted outcomes are also used to benchmark equivalence regions.
issues.quote: "We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography"

issues.subcategory: alcohol frequency operationalization mismatch
issues.description: The manuscript replaces the NIDA Quick Screen binge-oriented alcohol item with general alcohol frequency, while retaining broader addiction/problem measures. General drinking frequency is not equivalent to risky alcohol involvement and may be poorly aligned with moral disapproval of alcohol use or with problem symptomatology. This weakens the intended test of whether moral incongruence applies to recognized addictive disorders.
issues.quote: "for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed)."

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous nicotine measure
issues.description: A single tobacco/nicotine frequency item combines cigarettes, smokeless tobacco, and vaping/e-cigarettes, which differ in social acceptability, health risk, addiction profile, and moral valence. Lumping them may obscure meaningful differences and distort the interaction with moral disapproval.
issues.quote: "smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine."

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous illicit/prescription drug categories
issues.description: Broad categories such as "illegal/illicit drugs" and "prescription drugs for non-medical reasons" aggregate highly heterogeneous substances with very different use patterns, severity, and moral meanings. A single moral disapproval item and a single frequency item for each broad class are unlikely to validly capture the target constructs.
issues.quote: "Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons" ... "Illegal/Illicit Drugs"

issues.subcategory: different recall windows across predictors and outcomes
issues.description: Behavioral frequency is assessed over the past 12 months, whereas ASSIST problem items are over the past 3 months and BPS is over the past 6 months. This temporal mismatch weakens interpretability of regressions and interactions because predictors and outcomes reference different periods.
issues.quote: "past-year frequency" ... "In the past three months, how often..." ... "In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you"

issues.subcategory: restriction to users creates collider/range restriction problems
issues.description: Analyses appear to be limited to those endorsing past-year use for a given behavior in at least some sections. Conditioning on use may induce selection artifacts when moral disapproval also predicts use, and it restricts the frequency range. This can bias both main effects and interaction estimates, especially for stigmatized behaviors where disapprovers may be less likely to engage at all.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use."

issues.subcategory: underspecified handling of assumption violations
issues.description: The authors state they will run "supplemental analyses" when assumptions are violated, "as appropriate," and will prefer OLS if sign/significance is unchanged. This leaves wide researcher degrees of freedom because the alternative methods, decision rules, and reporting thresholds are not prespecified.
issues.quote: "in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate. Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results"

issues.subcategory: treating ordinal outcomes with OLS without clear justification
issues.description: Several dependent variables are ordinal sums/averages with limited categories and likely skewed distributions, especially for low-prevalence problems. The plan defaults to OLS moderation despite this, only vaguely mentioning robustness checks. This may yield biased estimates, heteroskedasticity, and confidence intervals inappropriate for bounded, zero-inflated outcomes.
issues.quote: "we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software"

issues.subcategory: inappropriate averaging of ASSIST items with different metric scales
issues.description: The ASSIST-derived outcome averages items scored 0-5 with items scored 0-3-6 and treats the result as a continuous mean. Because these items have different spacing and meanings, simple averaging assumes commensurability and equal weighting without validation. This can distort scale properties and comparability across substances.
issues.quote: "Participants will respond to three frequency based questions... on a scale of 0 ... to 5 ... Participants will also respond to two questions ... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged"

issues.subcategory: equivalence bound parameter inconsistency
issues.description: The equivalence test is introduced with SESOI of δ = .27, but later the same section says the equivalence region is set to β = .11 and repeatedly refers to δ = |.11|. It is unclear which bound is preregistered for the primary equivalence test. This ambiguity materially affects conclusions about whether effects are practically null.
issues.quote: "We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression ... with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27." ... "we elected to set our SESOI (δ) ... (β=.11" ... "setting our equivalence region to δ= |.11|"

issues.subcategory: mixing incomparable effect-size metrics to justify SESOI
issues.description: The manuscript justifies the equivalence region by citing ΔR2, f2, Cohen's d, and standardized β from different studies and measures, then selecting one value. These effect sizes are not directly interchangeable without assumptions, and using disparate metrics from different models and outcomes to define a single SESOI is methodologically unsound.
issues.quote: "Prior studies ... found moral incongruence to have small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen’s d = .24 ...), to moderate (ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen’s d = .69 ...), to relatively large (ΔR2 = .12, f2 = .23, Cohen’s d = .97 ...) ... we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above"

issues.subcategory: post hoc redefinition of equivalence region
issues.description: The analytic plan explicitly proposes changing the equivalence region after observing the pornography effect if initial hypotheses fail. This makes the test outcome-dependent and undermines the confirmatory logic of the preregistration. Post hoc calibration to observed data inflates interpretive flexibility.
issues.quote: "we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome."

issues.subcategory: outcome-dependent fallback analyses for low power
issues.description: For underpowered subgroups, the authors plan to switch from testing equivalence to a looser comparison against a large prior pornography effect. This changes the inferential target after seeing available subgroup sizes and makes confirmatory conclusions contingent on feasibility rather than a fixed hypothesis test.
issues.quote: "Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly... we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography"

issues.subcategory: power analysis inconsistent with actual sample design and subgroup Ns
issues.description: Power calculations are presented for regression models with six predictors and one tested predictor, but key analyses are run separately within behavior-specific user subsets, likely with skewed outcomes and potentially weighted/complex sampling. The calculations therefore may not reflect actual power. The manuscript itself acknowledges very low power for some subgroups, which undermines planned null/equivalence claims.
issues.quote: "All analyses conducted using G*power; assuming α = 0.05, regression models with 6 independent variables ... and 1 tested predictor." ... "Prescription Drug Misuse | Effective N | 140 | ... Estimated Achieved power for f2= .015 | .301"

issues.subcategory: underpowered rare-substance subgroups for null/equivalence claims
issues.description: The study is explicitly underpowered for prescription drug misuse and likely illicit drugs, yet hypotheses assert null interaction effects for these domains. Low power is especially problematic for equivalence testing because failing to reject a nonzero effect is not evidence of absence. The fallback strategy does not solve this for the original hypotheses.
issues.quote: "it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small"

issues.subcategory: no multiplicity control for primary analyses
issues.description: The plan includes at least eight moderation analyses, plus direct effects, correlations, equivalence tests, and likely secondary outcomes, but does not specify any familywise or false-discovery control for confirmatory hypothesis testing. Holm adjustment is mentioned only for bivariate correlations, not primary models.
issues.quote: "Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics" ... "In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses"

issues.subcategory: equivalence testing on standardized effects not clearly specified
issues.description: The manuscript states that equivalence decisions will be based on the confidence interval for the "observed standardized effect" of the interaction, but the analysis is described using lm on raw variables processed in SPSS. It is unclear whether coefficients, variables, or outcomes are standardized, and how confidence intervals for standardized interaction terms will be obtained. This is essential for reproducibility and for interpreting the equivalence bound.
issues.quote: "key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS" ... "Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction ... fall fully within our equivalence region"

issues.subcategory: missing exact model formulas and coding details
issues.description: The manuscript does not fully specify model equations, coding of gender categories beyond one binary contrast, treatment of nonbinary respondents, whether age is linear, whether sample-source indicator is included, or whether interactions with oversample status are tested. These omissions impede replication and interpretation.
issues.quote: "gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male), age, and overall religiousness included as covariates of the outcome."

issues.subcategory: problematic gender coding
issues.description: Coding gender as male versus "not-male" collapses women and nonbinary/other respondents into one category, creating a substantively uninterpretable covariate and potential misclassification. This is especially problematic for sexuality-related behaviors, which often vary by gender identity and sex.
issues.quote: "gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)"

issues.subcategory: causal/diagnostic overreach from cross-sectional self-reports
issues.description: The discussion of implications repeatedly suggests that finding a unique interaction would support the validity of the PPMI model and the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in ICD-11, and failure could imply systematic bias in addiction self-reports. A single cross-sectional survey with self-report measures cannot validate diagnostic criteria or establish the source of symptom reports.
issues.quote: "this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model" ... "there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD."

issues.subcategory: claims about bias and false positives without criterion validation
issues.description: The manuscript claims that if moral incongruence predicts self-reports across domains, self-reported symptoms in community samples may be systematically biased and may create false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings. However, there is no external criterion of actual disorder, clinician assessment, or functional impairment independent of self-report. Thus the study cannot determine false positives or bias in diagnostic classification.
issues.quote: "it would suggest that community and population-based research using self-reported symptoms of addiction might be systematically biased by participant morality." ... "whether it creates false-positive diagnoses in clinical settings."

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounding in observational comparisons
issues.description: Primary models include only age, gender, and religiousness as covariates. Many plausible confounds could influence both moral disapproval and self-reported addiction/problem scores, such as political ideology, mental distress, shame proneness, conservatism, abstinence attempts, relationship conflict, or treatment history. Sparse adjustment weakens any interpretation that moral incongruence has a unique role.
issues.quote: "In each case, we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates"

issues.subcategory: religiousness composite may not match moral conservatism
issues.description: The paper often links religiousness to conservative sexual values and appears to use religiousness as a key covariate or proxy for moral background. Yet the composite consists of prayer, attendance, and importance of religion, which may not validly capture moral conservatism or disapproval of specific behaviors. This weakens theoretical interpretation of covariate-adjusted effects.
issues.quote: "religiousness—especially conservative religiousness—is often a marker of such values." ... "Religiousness will be measured via the average of standardized responses to three items taken from Pew Research Center"

issues.subcategory: different outcome windows confound domain comparison
issues.description: Pornography problems are measured with a 6-month BPS, gambling with a 12-month PGSI, and substance ASSIST items largely with 3-month symptom windows. Domain differences in recall period can alter prevalence and effect size, making direct comparison of interaction magnitudes problematic.
issues.quote: "In the last 6 months" ... "Thinking about the last 12 months" ... "In the past three months"

issues.subcategory: no plan for reliability/validity of modified scales
issues.description: Although internal consistency will be reported, there is no prespecified plan to evaluate dimensionality, measurement invariance, or validity of heavily modified instruments and novel composites. Alpha/omega alone are insufficient for scales modified across content domains and response formats.
issues.quote: "Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total), will be calculated"

issues.subcategory: unwarranted assumption of no missing data
issues.description: The authors state they anticipate no unplanned missingness because YouGov quality controls are in place. This is unrealistic, especially for sensitive items on pornography, illicit drugs, and gambling. No missing-data handling method is specified, and listwise deletion or complete-case analysis could bias results if missingness is related to stigma or severity.
issues.quote: "Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data."

issues.subcategory: no details on item nonresponse or skip patterns
issues.description: Given contradictory statements about whether all respondents complete all measures, the manuscript should specify skip logic, expected structural missingness, and how nonusers' scores are treated. Without this, effective sample sizes and comparability across measures cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: "Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use." ... "key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior."

issues.subcategory: unclear use of validated versus modified outcomes for primary hypotheses
issues.description: The manuscript states pornography and gambling will be assessed using validated measures, but Table 1 also lists modified ASSIST outcomes for those same behaviors, and later exploratory comparisons refer specifically to the modified ASSIST pornography outcome. It is unclear which outcome is primary for confirmatory tests, opening room for selective emphasis.
issues.quote: "with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use" ... Table 1: "Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items" ... "using the modified NIDA-ASSIST items for pornography"

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale reported inconsistently
issues.description: The main text says BPS items are scored 0-2, whereas the supplemental materials show 0-2-4 scoring. This discrepancy affects total score range, comparability to validation studies, and any regression scaling or standardization.
issues.quote: "on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed." ... Supplemental: "Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)"

issues.subcategory: PGSI response coding inconsistent with standard and text
issues.description: The main text describes PGSI responses as 0 to 3, but the supplemental materials show 0, 2, 4, 5. This is a major inconsistency because it changes scoring and validity. If the nonstandard coding is used, the measure is altered without justification; if not, the supplement is wrong and not replicable.
issues.quote: "This 9-item measure requires participants to respond ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always)." ... Supplemental: "Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)"

issues.subcategory: alcohol binge item typo/manuscript error
issues.description: The male alcohol screening item in the supplement says "More than four drinks" despite the instruction stating more than 5 drinks on one occasion. This indicates poor instrument quality control and creates ambiguity about the actual administered item.
issues.quote: "IF GENDER = MAN ... In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)"

issues.subcategory: supplement/table corruption impedes reproducibility
issues.description: Table 2 appears duplicated/repeated in a corrupted format, and several supplemental tables repeat content or contain malformed coding. Such errors prevent independent verification of planned power analyses and instrument scoring.
issues.quote: "1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey ..." repeated multiple times within Table 2 cells

issues.subcategory: hypotheses framed to demonstrate uniqueness rather than test alternatives
issues.description: The introduction explicitly states a goal of demonstrating uniqueness of moral incongruence for sexual behavior. This wording suggests confirmatory bias and asymmetrical interpretation, especially given acknowledged evidence that moral disapproval predicts self-perceived problems in nonsexual domains. Registered reports should neutrally test competing hypotheses rather than aim to demonstrate a favored conclusion.
issues.quote: "with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors."

issues.subcategory: misinterpretation of interaction as proof of incongruence effects
issues.description: Even if the moral disapproval × frequency interaction is statistically significant for pornography but not other domains, that would not by itself establish that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior; differences could reflect measurement reliability, prevalence, scaling, or stigma intensity. The manuscript overstates what comparative interaction coefficients can show.
issues.quote: "should we find that moral incongruence—defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior—only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model"

issues.subcategory: correlation reporting with Holm-adjusted test statistics unclear/incorrect terminology
issues.description: The manuscript says correlations will be reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics. Holm adjustment applies to p-values, not test statistics. This may reflect imprecise or incorrect reporting of the planned procedure.
issues.quote: "Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics"

issues.subcategory: no preregistered decision rule for combining national and oversample data
issues.description: The manuscript does not state whether the representative sample and sports-wagering oversample will be pooled, analyzed separately, or meta-analyzed. Given the distinct recruitment frames, this is a critical omission for interpreting all gambling-related and pooled domain comparisons.
issues.quote: "we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports"

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding irrelevant but no protection against hypothesis-aware analysis
issues.description: As a registered report, the key protection should be strict analytic prespecification. Yet several central decisions remain flexible (assumption handling, equivalence region fallback, outcome choice), leaving room for confirmation-consistent analyses despite preregistration.
issues.quote: "Should results of moderation analyses remain robust ... we will present OLS results" ... "we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence"
